title: germanys far right is slow burning economic risk 2026 09 07
author: Jon Sindreu
text:
LONDON, Sept 7 (Reuters Breakingviews) - For a German economy emerging from a long lull, electoral success for the Alternative for Germany (AfD) represents less a spanner in the engine than a ​slow oil leak. Despite the far-right party's gains in a state election, manufacturing is back into expansion territory, ‌with €120 billion of public investment lined up for both this year and next, alongside a 12-year €500 billion infrastructure fund and a surge in defence spending. Nevertheless, the growing appeal of a party that is anti-immigration, sympathetic to Russia, seeks to leave the European Union and is sceptical of industrial policy carries ​significant long-term risks for Europe's largest economy.
The AfD came first in this weekend's election in Saxony-Anhalt, more than doubling its vote ​share in the state to 44%, while support for Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats slumped to ⁠just 17%. If the party forms a regional government, it would be the first time the German far right gains power since ​World War Two. It also leads polls in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, which holds an election later this month.
The AfD's success in Eastern German strongholds ​will not shift the balance of power in Germany's Bundesrat, or federal council. The direct economic impact is also limited: the two regions combined account for only 3.2% of national output. With the AfD also leading national opinion polls, though, Merz's colleagues and coalition partners in Berlin may lose their nerve. ​The already-unpopular chancellor risks joining reform-minded leaders, including Britain's Keir Starmer and Canada's Justin Trudeau, who were pushed out by their own ​parties.
Even such a change would probably have a limited economic effect. German GDP is expected to expand 0.6% this year and top 1% next year, ‌according ⁠to median analyst forecasts compiled by LSEG Datastream. While consumer spending has weakened again due to the war in Iran, fiscal stimulus is offsetting this, with a large wave of procurement contracts moving down the supply chain. Domestic capital goods orders are rebounding strongly as years of neglect force firms to rebuild capacity. Indeed, much of the recent rebound is driven by a global manufacturing upswing, fueled in ​part by the artificial intelligence boom: ​trade has stopped being a ⁠drag, contributing 0.6 percentage points to second-quarter growth.
Admittedly, this doesn't fix structural challenges, which would require the coalition to make further-reaching changes to labour market regulations, pensions and planning. Moreover, Merz still needs ​to prove that his tougher stance on China will translate into a plan to fix challenges ​in the country's ⁠chemical and car industries. The paradox is that, by correctly seeing through a short-term economic boost, German voters could be steering the country towards a darker and less prosperous future.
